prompt: There is an index on `orders(ordered_on)`, but `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ordered_on >= '2021-01-01'` uses a Seq Scan. The filter matches 847,258 of 1,000,000 rows. Why?

options.text: The index is corrupt and needs REINDEX
options.explanation: The same index was used for narrower date ranges. The planner simply chose not to use it for this one.

options.text: Postgres can't use B-tree indexes for `>=`
options.explanation: B-trees support range comparisons; the index served a one-quarter range in the same lesson.
The estimate was 846,113 rows against 847,258 actual, which is very accurate. The planner estimated the matching count closely.

options.text: With 85% of rows matching, reading the whole table sequentially is cheaper than an index walk plus heap fetches
options.explanation: Correct. An index would read most of the index and then nearly every heap page anyway, at higher cost per page. The seq scan reads 7,353 pages once, in order.

workedExample:
1. Matching rows: 85%.
2. An index scan would read ~85% of the index entries and fetch rows from virtually every heap page (each page holds ~136 rows).
3. A seq scan reads every page once, sequentially, at `seq_page_cost = 1` instead of `random_page_cost = 4`.

For this illustrative wide-row range query, the estimated sequential scan is cheaper. Indexes can also help broad queries by supplying order or covering their output columns.

prompt: Each heap page of `orders` holds about 136 rows. A filter on `ordered_on` matches 3.7% of rows, and orders for any date range are scattered randomly through the table. Before running anything, what do you predict a Bitmap Heap Scan for this filter will report under `Heap Blocks`?

options.text: About 3.7% of the table's pages, because 3.7% of the rows match
options.explanation: That would only hold if matching rows were packed together on the same pages, as in a table physically ordered by date. Scattered rows land on most pages.

options.text: About a third of the pages
options.explanation: There is nothing special about a third. With about five matching rows per page on average, very few pages have none at all.

options.text: Nearly all of the pages, because a typical page holds about five matching rows
options.explanation: Correct. 136 rows × 3.7% is about five matches per page, so a page with no match at all is rare (about 1 in 170). In the illustrative plan, 7,306 of 7,353 pages were visited.

options.text: Exactly one page per matching row
options.explanation: A bitmap scan visits each matching page once, however many matching rows it holds, so pages are far fewer than rows here; but that still means nearly every page.

workedExample:
1. Expected matches per page: about 136 × 3.7%, roughly five.
2. With rows scattered at random, a page escapes only if all of its 136 rows miss. With five expected matches, that is rare: about 1 page in 170.
3. So the scan must visit about 99% of the pages, even though only 3.7% of the rows match.

This is why physical-order correlation matters so much: with orders clustered by date, the same 3.7% of rows would occupy about 3.7% of the pages, and the index would save most of the reading. It is also why the planner may prefer a sequential scan for what looks like a selective filter.
